Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) which was conducted in the Microgravity Science Glovebox on the International Space Station (ISS) during Expedition 15.

one_line: On the Space Station, small pieces of common spacecraft materials (Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, cotton lamp wick) were overheated without burning, and the size of the smoke particles was measured to find out what kind of smoke detector would reliably catch an early spacecraft fire.
summary: SAME characterised pre-fire smoke in microgravity to guide spacecraft smoke-detector design. In the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox during Expedition 15 (2007), wire-wrapped samples of Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, cellulose lamp wick and a reference liquid (dibutyl phthalate on a wick) were heated below ignition in a 2-8 cm/s air flow; the smoke was held in an aging chamber for 10-1800 s, then measured by three compact instruments giving the zeroth, first and third moments of the size distribution, from which a lognormal geometric mean diameter and spread were derived. Fresh smoke had geometric mean diameters of 80-189 nm and mass-mean diameters of 179-472 nm (geometric standard deviation 1.84-2.18); 720 s of aging, by coagulation, raised these to 155-352 nm and 267-606 nm. Silicone and lamp-wick smoke carried roughly half their mass above 1 um; Teflon and Kapton very little. At matched 8 cm/s flow, sizes matched 1-g tests. The Shuttle ionization detector responded to every test, the ISS light-scattering detector poorly to Teflon. The investigators concluded single-moment detectors are risky and recommended multi-moment or size-classifying detection.

question.text: Spacecraft smoke detectors (ionization on the Space Shuttle, near-infrared forward light scattering on the US ISS modules) were designed from 1-g data, and the two designs respond to non-overlapping particle sizes. Without buoyancy, smoke from an overheated material stays longer in the hot, vapour-rich zone near the source and takes longer to reach a detector, so particles might grow by nucleation, condensation and coagulation. The earlier Shuttle-glovebox Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD) experiment had found larger solid smoke particles in low gravity and a Shuttle detector that was blind to visible silicone-rubber and paper smoke, but could not size the liquid droplets. SAME set out to quantify the particle size distribution of smoke from overheated (not flaming) spacecraft materials in microgravity, including the effect of sample temperature, air flow and aging time, to compare it with 1 g, to test the hypothesis that liquid smokes form substantially larger droplets in microgravity, and to evaluate how the two existing US spacecraft detectors respond.

physics.text: Smoke from a heated but unignited polymer is an aerosol of recondensed pyrolysis products: solid recondensed polymer (Teflon, Kapton) or liquid droplets (silicone rubber, paper/cellulose). Its size distribution is set near the source by homogeneous nucleation of supersaturated vapour, condensational growth and coagulation, and is then modified during transport by coagulation (number falls, mean size rises, mass is conserved) and by wall losses. On Earth the buoyant plume dilutes and carries away the vapour within a fraction of a second; in microgravity the only flow is the imposed or ventilation flow, so residence time at high concentration near the source and transit time to a detector both increase, which favours larger particles. Detectors respond to different moments of the distribution: an ionization chamber signal scales roughly with the first moment (total diameter per unit volume), a light-scattering detector with roughly the third moment (mass) for particles of about 0.2-2 um, so the same smoke can look strong to one and weak to the other. SAME exploited this by measuring three moments and assuming a lognormal distribution, which is fully defined by number concentration, geometric mean diameter and geometric standard deviation. The investigators' CFD model of the ISS Destiny lab showed that, without buoyancy, ventilation mixes smoke through the module instead of collecting it at a ceiling, so detection times are longer and depend on source location.

apparatus.text: An MSG payload assembled by the crew from modular units (about 5 h of crew time) and then run largely from the GRC Telescience Center. Each sample was a roughly 3 mm diameter cylinder of material wrapped in a stainless-steel wire coil that both heated it and, through its resistance, measured and controlled its temperature (setpoints expressed as a resistance ratio Rt/R0: Kapton 1.380, lamp wick 1.245, silicone 1.327, Teflon 1.440). Six pre-weighed samples were mounted per carousel; five carousels were flown. A piston in a 5.65 L aging chamber drew air over the heated sample through the smoke generation tube (design range 2-8 cm/s; software maximum 9.8 cm/s), held the smoke for a set time with a mixing fan, then pushed it into a low-volume diagnostics duct. There the smoke was measured by: a TSI P-Trak condensation particle counter (isopropanol condensation, 20 nm to about 1 um, 0-1e5 cm^-3, after a software-controlled dynamic diluter; condenser grooved for microgravity), a First Alert residential ionization chamber (Am-241), two TSI DustTraks (90-degree red-laser scattering, 0.001-100 mg/m^3) with 1 um and 10 um inlet impactors, plus an ISS laser forward-scattering detector and a Space Shuttle ionization detector with inertial separator. Thermal precipitators sampled smoke onto TEM grids before and after aging. Signals were digitized at 1 Hz (8-bit).

procedure.text: For each test point the ground team uplinked parameters (sample, heater setpoint, flow, aging time, diagnostics and dilution); the carousel rotated a new sample into the flow duct; the sample was heated for about 60 s (75 s in one run) below its ignition point while the retreating piston drew the smoke-laden air into the aging chamber. After the chosen aging time (10 s to 1800 s) the piston pushed the smoke through the diagnostics duct, where the moment instruments and the two spacecraft detectors sampled it; for aging runs the smoke was measured before and after aging. TEM grids were exposed in the thermal precipitators, and samples were weighed before launch and after return. DustTrak response was calibrated on the ground for each smoke source against a tapered element oscillating microbalance; P-Trak and ionization chamber were calibrated with monodisperse dioctyl phthalate (DOP) droplets against reference instruments. D_0.5 and D_1.5 were computed per run and converted to D_g and sigma_g assuming a lognormal distribution. Ground (1 g) comparison runs were made afterwards with the same type of hardware. Dibutyl phthalate samples were reheated repeatedly to obtain extra test points.

psi_data.summary: PSI holds the documents needed to understand SAME: a 68-page final science report (2010) that appends the four SAE/AIAA papers of 2008-2009 and the flight test log, the requirements document (EIRD) with the CSD background and design calculations, a concept description, operations manual, software and crew-interface documents, and two readable 2012-2013 presentations that actually belong to the SAME reflight era (SAME-2). The 59 readable analyzed-data spreadsheets are per-run 1 Hz housekeeping and diagnostic time series (P-Trak, two DustTraks, two ionization channels, ISS and STS detector voltages, heater resistance, flows) for most of the 47 test points, some with averaging windows marked, plus command logs. They contain no computed particle diameters and no calibration curves, so re-deriving the size table requires the ground calibrations, which are not in PSI. The 8-row experimental table reproduces the pre-flight planning matrix, not the as-flown conditions. Three legacy .ppt files and one .doc are unreadable, and 18 engineering drawings have no text layer.

findings.claim: Holding the smoke for 720 s raised all mean sizes and narrowed the distribution, consistent with coagulation. Geometric mean diameter rose to 155 nm (Kapton, x1.9), 258 nm (lamp wick, x1.4), 352 nm (silicone, x1.9) and 228 nm (Teflon, x1.3). Diameter of average mass rose by 28-49%, to 267-606 nm, and sigma_g fell to 1.81-1.83 for all four materials. During aging the P-Trak number count fell substantially while DustTrak mass stayed nearly constant, which indicates coagulation with little wall loss.

findings.claim: The later flight-versus-ground comparison (SAME-2 presentation, 2013) reached a weaker conclusion than the 2008 analysis. At 8 cm/s, ground tests gave particle dimensions very close to the flight results, and particle size grew substantially as air flow was reduced. Imposed flow and residence time, rather than gravity as such, appear to control the size. The PSI documents do not reconcile the two statements, and the 2013 deck may include SAME-R flight data. The investigators' 2018 Fire Safety Journal paper, which covers both flights (2007 and 2010), settles it in favour of the weaker conclusion: low-gravity smoke was not significantly different from smoke made under equivalent 1-g conditions, and flight and ground diameters of average mass at matched flow, temperature and aging fall on a slope-1 line at 8.1 cm/s. Lower flow could raise the diameter of average mass by up to about a factor of 2. The preliminary 50% figure in findings[4] is therefore superseded.

findings.claim: The Space Shuttle ionization detector, sensitive below about 1 um, gave strong signals in every SAME test, including the larger-particle lamp wick and silicone smokes. The ISS forward-scattering detector, sensitive above about 0.5 um, gave strong signals for silicone rubber but erratic or weak signals for Teflon (and Kapton) smoke, which is mostly below 1 um. The two US spacecraft detector designs therefore respond differently to realistic pre-fire smokes.

The SAME data therefore bound the problem but do not span it.

findings.claim: Implication for detector design: any detector that measures a single moment either needs a very large number concentration to alarm on small particles or alarms on very few large particles, such as dust. The investigators showed this with a hypothetical single-point alarm requirement of 2 mg/m^3 for a lognormal aerosol with GMD 500 nm and sigma_g 1.3. They recommended alarm requirements at several sizes across roughly 200-1200 nm and detectors that measure two or more moments or classify particles by size, which would also help reject false alarms.

sources.quote: These figures were developed assuming the alarm level was set at 2 mg/m 3 for a log-normal particle size distribution with a 500 nm geometric mean diameter (GMD) and a geometric standard deviation (GSD) of 1.3.
Consequently a specification for a single particle size (or no size specification) would be risky.
An alternative is to develop alarm requirements that include criteria at particle sizes spanning the expected range of fire particulate (e.g. 200 to 1200 nm).

Two possible effective means of achieving this size discrimination are to employ a detector that measures more than one mo ment of the size distribution or to use a detector that can classify the particles into size ranges.

findings.claim: Spacecraft background aerosol is sparse at small sizes: ISS US-lab counts measured by the precursor DAFT experiment were below 5 particles/cm^3, the instrument noise level. STS-32 impactors found about 40% of particles in each of the 2.5-10 um and >100 um ranges. This leaves a sub-micrometre detection window where pyrolysis smoke dominates. Because aging and slow mixing make smoke grow, the investigators cautioned against designing only for small particles.

sources.quote: the particle count levels were at the noise level for the instrument (less than 5 particles/cm 3).
The two impactors reported a bimodal particle size distribution with ~ 40% of the particles in each of the 2.5 μm to 10 μm and >100 μm ranges.
Given the effects of aging and the slow mixing seen in spacecraft, it is probably unwise to focus entirely on small particle sizes for fire detection

findings.claim: A companion FDS (Fire Dynamics Simulator) model of smoke transport in the ISS Destiny lab, with g = 0 and propane sources giving 1.46-8.47 mg/s of particulate, found that ventilation mixes smoke fairly uniformly through the module. Detection times by the two area detectors (alarm about 0.5 mg/m^3) were long and depended strongly on source location and on obstructions. Some low-soot-yield cases never alarmed.

sources.quote: The alarm point for the ISS detector is on the order of 0.5 mg/m 3.
Numerical modeling of smoke transport in the US Lab Module of the ISS predicted that actual detection times can be quite long and strongly dependent on lo cation and the presence of obstructions.
Note that a DNA (did not alarm) condition occurred for LA1 for the 0.05 soot yield on the N1 wall for LAS5RR and for LA3 0.05 soot yield on the S3 wall for LAP1RR.

findings.claim: Method: the moment method (three compact instruments plus a lognormal assumption) worked inside the MSG volume and produced on-orbit size statistics without sample return. Uncertainty propagation shows the first-moment (ionization chamber) error dominates the uncertainty in D_g and sigma_g, while the third-moment error matters least. An early Mie-scattering inversion of the DustTrak signal failed to converge for some runs (all silicone baseline runs in the 2009 AIAA paper), possibly because of bimodal distributions. relevance.text: SAME is the main microgravity data set behind requirements for next-generation spacecraft smoke detectors. Its central message is that early (pre-flaming) smoke from common spacecraft materials spans roughly 100 nm to beyond 1 um and shifts with material, flow and aging. Teflon and Kapton smoke stays mostly below 300 nm and is hard for light-scattering detectors such as the ISS unit to see. Silicone and cellulose smoke puts much of its mass above 1 um, where ionization detectors with particle separators, such as the Shuttle unit, may lose it (as in CSD). Smoke trapped in enclosures or carried slowly by cabin ventilation coarsens by coagulation. Background dust is mostly large, so a detector that measures two moments, or classifies by size, can both catch small-particle smoke and reject dust. Transferability: these are small, controlled, non-flaming overheat events of four materials at 2-8 cm/s and up to 30 min aging. They are not flaming fires (soot), not full-scale cabin fires, and the gravity effect itself is uncertain because ground tests at matched flow gave similar sizes.

habitat_conditions.text: No PSI document states the oxygen fraction or pressure of the air drawn over the samples. The smoke was generated in air inside the MSG on ISS, nominally cabin air, but this is not documented. Against the common references: Earth sea level is 20.9% O2 at 101.3 kPa; a Moon habitat would likely have 30% O2 or more at 70.3 kPa or less; a spacesuit has 100% O2 at 29.6 kPa. SAME gives no data on how oxygen enrichment or reduced pressure would change pyrolysis rate, nucleation or particle size, or on how lower pressure (longer mean free path, faster coagulation and diffusion) would affect detector response. Its results apply to near-sea-level air only by assumption. There is also no partial-gravity smoke data.

earth_benefits.text: The investigators expect the smoke-detector technology to be useful in other confined, extreme environments on Earth, such as submarines and underwater laboratories. The multi-moment detection concept also addresses the familiar trade-off between ionization and photoelectric residential detectors.

limitations.text: Size statistics rest on a lognormal assumption from three moments. Bimodal distributions (suspected for silicone) cannot be represented, and the third-moment instrument depends strongly on particle size and refractive index. The final DustTrak calibration assumed each smoke's size distribution matched its ground calibration aerosol.

limitations.text: Published values changed between analyses. Teflon baseline GMD was 159 nm (AIAA 2009) and 170 nm (final report), and its diameter of average mass 219 and 297 nm. Lamp wick diameter of average mass was 420 and 341 nm. Silicone count mean diameter was 263, 227 and 257 nm in the three papers. The 2012 SAME-1&2 table gives much smaller unaged values, for example Kapton GMD 47 nm. Absolute sizes therefore carry a calibration uncertainty of tens of percent.

The final report's text says the aged silicone diameter of average mass rose to over 1 um. Its own table (606 nm) and the 2009 ICES paper ('over 500 nm') contradict this, so the 1 um statement looks like an error.

It is not the as-flown test list: the flight used 2-8 cm/s, aging of 10-1800 s and 47 test points (final report Appendix A).
Sample O2 fraction and pressure are not stated anywhere in the PSI documents examined (final report, EIRD, concept description, operations manual).

Sample temperatures in degrees C, measured mass-loss rates, per-run flow velocities and aging times are not tabulated. Only the heater Rt/R0 setpoints and a few log comments (2 cm/s, 30 min aging, 75 s heating) were found.
